q: Which of the following neurological conditions is NOT classified as a neurodegenerative disorder?
concept: The answer is epilepsy because, unlike the other three, it is not a neurodegenerative disorder but a paroxysmal condition characterised by recurrent, unprovoked seizures arising from abnormal, excessive, synchronous electrical discharges in the brain. Neurodegenerative disorders share a defining feature: a progressive, ongoing loss or death of neurons over time, so the person steadily worsens as brain tissue is lost. Parkinson's disease progressively destroys dopamine neurons in the substantia nigra, producing tremor, rigidity, and bradykinesia; Alzheimer's disease progressively kills cortical and hippocampal neurons through amyloid and tau pathology, producing worsening memory loss and dementia; and Huntington's disease, an inherited disorder caused by an expanded CAG trinucleotide repeat on chromosome 4, progressively degenerates neurons in the striatum, producing chorea and cognitive decline. Epilepsy is fundamentally different: between seizures the brain can function normally, the condition is defined by episodic electrical dysfunction rather than steady cell death, and many people with epilepsy have it controlled for life without progressive deterioration. Although very severe or prolonged seizures can cause some secondary damage, epilepsy is categorised as a seizure disorder, not a degenerative one. The exam skill for 'NOT' questions is to name the shared property (here, progressive neuronal loss) and pick the item that lacks it.

traps.a: Parkinson's disease is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder caused by loss of dopamine-producing neurons in the substantia nigra, so it does not fit the 'NOT' the question asks for.
traps.b: Alzheimer's disease is the classic neurodegenerative dementia marked by amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles, so it is not the exception being sought.
traps.d: Huntington's disease is a hereditary neurodegenerative disorder from a CAG-repeat mutation causing progressive loss of striatal neurons, so it too is genuinely degenerative.

q: Who gave the theory of cognitive dissonance?
concept: The answer is c: Leon Festinger gave the theory of cognitive dissonance. In A Theory of Cognitive Dissonance, Leon Festinger (1957) proposed that holding two cognitions that contradict each other (beliefs, attitudes or knowledge of one's own behaviour) creates an unpleasant state of tension, dissonance, which people are motivated to reduce. They can change the behaviour, change one of the beliefs, add new consonant beliefs, or play down the importance of the conflict. The classic test is the study by Festinger and James Carlsmith (1959). Students spent an hour on dull tasks such as turning pegs, then were paid either $1 or $20 to tell the next participant that the tasks were enjoyable. Afterwards, those paid $1 rated the tasks as more enjoyable than those paid $20. Twenty dollars was enough to justify the lie, but one dollar was not, so the $1 group reduced their dissonance by changing their attitude: the effect of insufficient justification. Dissonance also explains effort justification (we value what we suffered to get) and post-decision dissonance (we upgrade the option we chose). For example, Vikram smokes but knows that smoking causes cancer. He may quit, or he may tell himself 'my grandfather smoked and lived to 90', adding a consonant cognition that eases the tension. Option c is right because the theory, its name and its founding experiments are Festinger's. Exam trap: Daryl Bem's self-perception theory (1967) explains the same $1 versus $20 result without any tension, by people inferring their attitudes from their own behaviour; Bem, or Fritz Heider's balance theory (1946), is the usual near miss for the founder of dissonance theory.

traps.a: Rensis Likert (1932) devised the summated rating attitude scale (strongly agree to strongly disagree); he measured attitudes rather than explaining dissonance.
traps.b: Leonard Doob was one of the Yale group (John Dollard, Doob, Neal Miller, O. Hobart Mowrer and Robert Sears, 1939) behind the frustration-aggression hypothesis and wrote on attitudes and propaganda; dissonance theory is not his.
traps.d: Option c correctly names Leon Festinger, so 'none of the above' cannot be right.

q: All of the following are used to study perceptual development EXCEPT
concept: The answer is b: the rod and frame apparatus is not a method for studying perceptual development. Researchers need ways to learn what a baby, who cannot speak, sees. Robert Fantz (1961) introduced preferential looking: two stimuli are shown side by side and an observer times how long the infant looks at each; a reliable preference shows the infant can tell them apart, and young infants looked longest at faces and patterns. Eleanor Gibson and Richard Walk (1960) built the visual cliff, a glass-topped table with a checkerboard just under the glass on the shallow side and far below on the deep side; most crawling infants aged 6 to 14 months refused to cross the deep side. Animal experiments allow control of early experience that would be unethical in children: Richard Held and Alan Hein's (1963) kitten carousel showed that kittens need self-produced movement to develop visually guided behaviour, Colin Blakemore and Grahame Cooper (1970) reared kittens seeing only vertical stripes, and Torsten Wiesel and David Hubel (1963) showed that closing one eye early permanently changes the visual cortex. The rod and frame test of Herman Witkin (1948 to 1954) is different: in a dark room a person sets a luminous rod to vertical inside a tilted luminous frame. Field-dependent people tilt the rod towards the frame; field-independent people trust their bodily sense of upright. It measures a cognitive style in older children and adults whose perception is already mature. Example: to learn whether 4-month-old Aarav can tell red from green, a researcher times his looks at the two colours side by side; the rod and frame test could not be given to him. Option b is right because the rod and frame test measures an individual difference in cognitive style, not how perception develops. Exam trap: the rod and frame test is a genuine perception task, so it looks as if it belongs; but it compares mature perceivers rather than tracing development.

q: Which of the following is not a method used in descriptive research?
concept: The answer is b: an experiment is not a descriptive method. Descriptive research aims to describe behaviour as it is: what happens, how often and in whom. It does not manipulate anything, so it cannot show cause and effect. Its main methods are the case study, the survey and naturalistic observation. A case study is an intensive study of one person or a small group, often over a long time. A survey asks a large sample questions through questionnaires or interviews, as in Alfred Kinsey's (1948) studies of sexual behaviour. Naturalistic observation records behaviour in its usual setting without interfering, as Jane Goodall (1960) did when she began watching chimpanzees at Gombe. An experiment is different in kind. The researcher manipulates an independent variable, controls other factors, ideally assigns participants to conditions at random, and measures the effect on a dependent variable. It is the only method that can establish causation. For example, Meera wants to study students' screen time. Watching them in the canteen or surveying 500 students describes their habits. Randomly assigning half of them to a no-phone week and comparing their sleep with the other half is an experiment. Option b is right because experiments test causes by manipulating variables, while the other three only describe. Exam trap: correlational studies are sometimes grouped with descriptive research because they also manipulate nothing, and a 'field experiment' takes place in a natural setting but is still an experiment, not naturalistic observation.

traps.a: A case study is an in-depth description of one person or group, such as Sigmund Freud's case histories; it describes but does not manipulate.
traps.c: A survey describes the attitudes or behaviour of a sample through questionnaires or interviews, as in Alfred Kinsey's work; it is a classic descriptive method.
traps.d: Naturalistic observation describes behaviour in its natural setting without interference, as in Jane Goodall's chimpanzee studies; nothing is manipulated.

q: Multimodal therapy assesses a person's:
concept: The answer is b: multimodal therapy assesses a person's BASIC I.D. Arnold Lazarus (1973), a South African-born clinical psychologist trained in behaviour therapy, argued that lasting change needs work across all the modalities of human functioning, and developed multimodal therapy, later set out in Multimodal Behavior Therapy (1976) and The Practice of Multimodal Therapy (1981). BASIC I.D. is an acronym for seven interacting modalities: Behaviour, Affect, Sensation, Imagery, Cognition, Interpersonal relationships, and Drugs/biology (medication, health, diet, exercise). The therapist builds a modality profile, listing problems and treatments under each heading, and may use 'bridging' (starting in the client's preferred modality before moving to an avoided one) and 'tracking' (noting the firing order of modalities, for example sensation, then cognition, then affect). Lazarus called his stance technical eclecticism: borrow effective techniques from any school while explaining them with one theory, social learning. Example: for Riya's panic attacks the profile might list avoiding the metro (behaviour), terror (affect), palpitations (sensation), images of fainting (imagery), the thought 'I am dying' (cognition), dependence on her brother (interpersonal) and too much coffee (drugs/biology), each with its own intervention. Option b is right because BASIC I.D. is the multimodal assessment framework itself. Exam trap: Arnold Lazarus (multimodal therapy) is often confused with Richard Lazarus, the stress and coping theorist (Stress, Appraisal, and Coping, 1984, with Susan Folkman).

traps.a: Cognitive functioning is only the C of BASIC I.D., one of seven modalities, so it is too narrow to describe the assessment.
traps.c: A biological profile is only the D (drugs and biology) modality; multimodal assessment covers six other areas as well.
traps.d: Overall intelligence is measured by IQ tests such as the Wechsler scales; it is not part of the multimodal assessment.

q: Dysthymic or Persistent depressive disorder (PDD) differs from major depressive disorder (MDD) in the following ways:

options.a: Symptoms include hallucinations and delusional thinking.
options.b: Symptoms only affect women during the winter months.
options.c: Symptoms are more severe and last longer.
options.d: Symptoms are less severe but last longer.

concept: The correct answer is that in dysthymia the symptoms are less severe but last longer. Persistent depressive disorder (PDD), the DSM-5 label that merged the older diagnoses of dysthymia and chronic major depression, is a chronic form of depression. Its defining contrast with major depressive disorder (MDD) is chronicity versus severity. MDD involves discrete major depressive episodes marked by more severe symptoms (such as pronounced anhedonia, significant appetite or sleep changes, and possibly suicidal ideation) that must last at least two weeks. Dysthymia or PDD, by contrast, involves milder but more enduring depressive symptoms (such as low mood, low energy, poor self-esteem, and hopelessness) that persist for at least two years in adults (or one year in children and adolescents), with symptom-free periods lasting no longer than two months. So the depressed mood in PDD is generally less intense than in a full major depressive episode but is far more chronic and long-lasting. A person can even experience a major depressive episode superimposed on dysthymia, historically called double depression. The distractors describe psychotic depression, seasonal affective disorder, and a reversed severity claim. This item tests the severity-versus-duration distinction between chronic and episodic depression.

traps.a: Hallucinations and delusions indicate psychotic features, which can occur in severe major depression but do not define dysthymia; dysthymia is milder, not psychotic.
traps.b: Symptoms confined to winter describe seasonal affective disorder (seasonal pattern), not dysthymia, and dysthymia is not sex-restricted.
traps.c: This reverses the relationship: dysthymia is less severe than MDD, not more severe, even though it is more chronic.

q: Which memory phenomenon suggests that recall is better when the retrieval context matches the encoding context?
concept: This question turns on Endel Tulving's encoding specificity principle, which holds that retrieval is most successful when the cues available at recall overlap with the information encoded at the time of learning. Context-dependent memory is the specific case where the external environment serves as one of those cues. The most famous demonstration came from Duncan Godden and Alan Baddeley in 1975, who had deep-sea divers learn word lists either on land or underwater and then recall them in the same or the opposite environment. Recall was substantially better when the learning and testing environments matched, even though the material itself was identical. The environment (sights, sounds, location) becomes bound to the memory trace during encoding, and reinstating it later provides retrieval cues that reactivate the trace. Note the careful distinction from state-dependent memory, which involves matching an internal physiological or emotional state rather than the outside setting. Both are corollaries of encoding specificity, but the stem explicitly names the retrieval context, meaning the external situation, so context-dependent memory is the precise fit. The practical lesson is that memory is not just about how strongly something was stored but about how well the conditions at recall reinstate the original encoding conditions, which is why studying in the room you will be tested in can genuinely help.

traps.a: The serial position effect describes better recall for items at the start and end of a list, not any matching of external context.
traps.c: State-dependent memory hinges on matching internal states such as mood or intoxication, not the external surroundings referred to here.
traps.d: Flashbulb memory (Roger Brown and James Kulik, 1977) concerns vivid, emotionally charged recollections of surprising events, not context-cue matching at retrieval.

q: The body's primary circadian pacemaker is the:
concept: The answer is c: the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) is the body's primary circadian pacemaker. A circadian rhythm (Latin circa diem, 'about a day') is a cycle of roughly 24 hours, such as sleep and waking, body temperature and hormone release. The SCN is a tiny pair of nuclei in the hypothalamus, sitting just above the optic chiasm, which gives it its name. Light reaches it directly from the retina along the retinohypothalamic tract, so daylight resets the clock each day; such resetting cues are called zeitgebers ('time givers'). The SCN in turn signals the pineal gland to release melatonin in darkness, which promotes sleep. The evidence is strong. In 1972 two teams (Robert Moore with Victor Eichler, and Friedrich Stephan with Irving Zucker) found that destroying the SCN in rats abolished their daily rhythms: the rats slept the usual total amount, but at random times. Martin Ralph (1990) and colleagues transplanted SCN tissue between hamsters, and the recipients took on the donor's rhythm. Even isolated SCN cells keep firing in a daily cycle, so the clock is built in. For example, when Kabir flies from Delhi to New York, his SCN is still set to Indian time, so he is wide awake at 3 a.m.; jet lag lasts until daylight resets his clock. Option c is right because the SCN generates the master 24-hour rhythm and keeps the body's other clocks in step. Exam trap: the pineal gland is the usual distractor because it secretes melatonin, the 'darkness hormone'. But the pineal only carries out the SCN's timing signal; the pacemaker itself is the SCN.

traps.a: The pineal gland secretes melatonin at night on the SCN's signal; it is an output of the clock, not the master pacemaker.
traps.b: The hippocampus is a limbic structure for consolidating memories and building spatial maps, not for timing daily rhythms.
traps.d: The amygdala is the limbic centre for fear, aggression and emotional memory; it plays no pacemaker role.

q: When conducting research on attribution theories, which type of attribution refers to the tendency to explain one's successes as a result of internal, stable factors, and failures as a result of external, situational factors?
concept: The answer is b: the self-serving attributional bias is the tendency to credit our successes to internal, stable causes and to blame our failures on external, situational ones. Attribution theory asks how ordinary people explain behaviour. Fritz Heider (1958) first split causes into internal (dispositional: ability, effort, character) and external (situational: luck, task difficulty, other people). Later research showed that our explanations are tilted, and this particular tilt depends on whether the outcome was good or bad. Dale Miller and Michael Ross (1975) reviewed the early studies and found the success half (taking credit) better supported than the failure half; a later meta-analysis by Amy Mezulis and colleagues (2004) confirmed that the bias is large and widespread, though smaller in many Asian cultures. The usual explanation is protection of self-esteem, helped by a wish to look good in front of others (self-presentation). For example, when Arjun tops his statistics test he says, 'I am good with numbers'; when he fails the next one he says, 'The paper was unfair and the invigilator kept disturbing us.' Option b is right because only the self-serving bias switches the direction of the explanation with the outcome: internal and stable for success, external and situational for failure. Exam trap: the fundamental attribution error also contrasts internal and external causes, but it concerns how we explain other people's behaviour (overrating their dispositions), not how we explain our own successes and failures.

traps.a: Dispositional attribution is one side of Fritz Heider's (1958) internal versus external distinction: explaining any behaviour by a person's traits or abilities. It names a type of cause, not a bias that switches between internal and external depending on success or failure.
traps.c: The fundamental attribution error, named by Lee Ross (1977), is overrating dispositions and underrating the situation when we explain other people's behaviour. The stem is about explaining one's own outcomes, and the pattern changes with success or failure, which the error does not.
traps.d: The covariation model is Harold Kelley's (1967) account of how we choose between causes using consensus, consistency and distinctiveness information. It is a rational model of how attribution should work, not a bias.

q: According to Jean Piaget's cognitive development theory, which cognitive limitation explains why a preoperational child believes that a tall, narrow glass holds more liquid than a short, wide glass, even after watching the liquid poured directly from one to the other ?
concept: The answer is c: the preoperational child fails liquid conservation because of centration and a lack of reversibility. Jean Piaget (1952), in The Child's Conception of Number, showed that young children do not grasp conservation, the understanding that a quantity stays the same when only its shape or arrangement changes. In the liquid task a child agrees that two identical short, wide glasses hold the same amount of juice. One is then poured, in full view, into a tall, narrow glass. A four- or five-year-old now says the tall glass has more. Two limits of preoperational thought (about 2 to 7 years) explain this. Centration is focusing on one striking feature, here the height of the liquid, while ignoring another, the narrower width. Lack of reversibility is the inability to run the action backwards in the mind and see that pouring the juice back would give equal glasses again. Around 7, in the concrete operational stage, children conserve and justify it with three arguments: identity (nothing was added or taken away), compensation (taller but thinner) and reversibility (pour it back and it is the same). Example: Riya, aged 4, insists her brother's tall glass of lassi has more than hers, though their mother poured both from the same jug; at 8 she laughs at the idea. Option c is right because centration plus irreversibility is Piaget's own explanation of conservation failure. Exam trap: lack of object permanence (b) sounds like losing track of things, but it is an infant limitation, solved by about 2 years, long before this task.

traps.a: Assimilation is Jean Piaget's term for fitting new information into an existing scheme; preoperational children assimilate constantly, so an inability to assimilate is not why they fail conservation.
traps.b: Object permanence, knowing that objects exist when out of sight, is a sensorimotor achievement complete by about 18 to 24 months, so a preoperational child already has it; the juice never leaves view in this task anyway.
traps.d: Formal deductive operations belong to the formal operational stage from about 11 or 12; missing them explains a younger child's trouble with abstract hypotheses, not failure to conserve, which concrete operations solve around 7.

q: In structural equation modeling (SEM), ______ is used to evaluate model fit.
concept: The answer is a: in structural equation modelling (SEM) the chi-square test is the basic test of model fit. SEM joins a measurement model (a confirmatory factor analysis linking observed items to latent variables) with a structural model (paths among those latent variables, extending the path analysis of Sewall Wright, 1921). Karl Jöreskog (1969 onwards, later with the LISREL program) made it practical. A model implies a particular pattern of variances and covariances, and fit asks how closely that implied matrix matches the one actually observed. The chi-square test of exact fit has the null hypothesis that the model reproduces the data perfectly, so the usual logic is reversed: a non-significant chi-square means good fit. Because chi-square grows with sample size, large samples make even trivial misfit significant, so researchers also report approximate fit indices: the comparative fit index (CFI) and Tucker-Lewis index (TLI), about .95 or above; the root mean square error of approximation (RMSEA), about .06 or below; and the standardised root mean square residual (SRMR), .08 or below (cut-offs from Li-tze Hu and Peter Bentler, 1999). Example: Kabir tests a model in which academic stress leads to rumination, which leads to depressive symptoms, each construct measured by three items, in 250 students. He obtains a non-significant chi-square, an RMSEA of .04 and a CFI of .97, and concludes that the model fits. Option a is right because chi-square is the classic statistic for judging how well an SEM reproduces the data. Exam trap: in SEM you want chi-square not to be significant, the opposite of most tests; and Cronbach's alpha, which also appears in SEM papers, checks the reliability of indicators, not fit.

traps.b: The Mann-Whitney U test (Henry Mann and Donald Whitney, 1947) is a non-parametric rank test comparing two independent groups, an alternative to the independent t-test; it plays no part in judging model fit.
traps.c: Cronbach's alpha (Lee Cronbach, 1951) estimates the internal consistency reliability of a scale; it is checked for indicators before an SEM, but it says nothing about whether the model fits.
traps.d: Cohen's d (Jacob Cohen, 1988) is a standardised mean difference between two groups, an effect size; it describes how big a difference is, not how well a covariance model reproduces the data.

q: Which of the following is a core principle of cognitive-behavioural therapy (CBT)?
concept: The answer is b: identifying and modifying dysfunctional thoughts is a core principle of cognitive-behavioural therapy (CBT). CBT rests on the cognitive model: it is not events themselves but how we interpret them that shapes our feelings and behaviour, and thoughts, emotions, bodily sensations and actions keep feeding one another. Two founders stand out: Albert Ellis, whose rational therapy (1955) became rational emotive behaviour therapy, and Aaron Beck, whose cognitive therapy grew from his research on depression. In Beck's approach therapist and client work in collaborative empiricism, treating thoughts as hypotheses to be tested rather than facts. Socratic questioning ('What is the evidence? Is there another way to see it?') guides the client to notice overlooked information. The dysfunctional thought record (1979) has columns for the situation, the emotion and its intensity, the automatic thought, a balanced response and the outcome. Behavioural experiments, activity scheduling and homework turn the new thinking into action, and sessions are structured, time-limited and focused on present problems. Example: a man with social anxiety thinks 'Everyone will see me sweating and think I am weird'; he records the thought, rates his belief at 90 percent, weighs the evidence and tests it by speaking at a meeting, after which his belief falls to 30 percent. Option b is right because cognitive restructuring of dysfunctional thoughts is the defining method of CBT. Exam trap: free association, dream analysis and resolving unconscious conflict are all psychoanalytic; CBT works with conscious, accessible thoughts in the present.

traps.a: Free association, the 'fundamental rule' of Freud's psychoanalysis, asks the patient to say whatever comes to mind without censoring it so that unconscious material surfaces; CBT does not use it.
traps.c: Dream analysis is Freud's 'royal road to the unconscious' (The Interpretation of Dreams, 1900), decoding the manifest content of a dream into its latent wishes; it belongs to psychoanalysis, not CBT.
traps.d: Unconscious conflict resolution is the aim of psychodynamic therapy, pursued through interpretation of resistance and transference; CBT targets conscious thoughts and present behaviour.

q: 'Nihilistic delusions' are commonly seen in
concept: A nihilistic delusion (delusion of negation) is a fixed false belief that oneself, part of one's body, other people or the whole world does not exist, has died, is rotting or has come to an end: 'my intestines have rotted away', 'I am already dead', 'my family no longer exists'. Jules Cotard (1880) described the extreme form, now called Cotard's syndrome, with delusions of being dead or of lacking organs, sometimes combined with a belief in being immortal and condemned to suffer forever. Nihilistic delusions are the classic mood-congruent delusion of severe depression, especially psychotic depression in older adults. DSM-5-TR uses the specifier 'with mood-congruent psychotic features' when delusional content matches depressive themes of personal inadequacy, guilt, disease, death, nihilism or deserved punishment, and ICD-11 codes a severe depressive episode with psychotic symptoms. Other delusions point to other disorders: grandiose delusions to mania; persecutory, referential, bizarre and passivity delusions to schizophrenia; non-bizarre, well-systematised delusions to delusional disorder. Nihilistic delusions can also occur in schizophrenia, dementia and other organic brain conditions, which is why the stem says 'commonly seen'. Clinically they signal severe illness, and refusal to eat by a patient who believes his stomach is gone can be dangerous; electroconvulsive therapy is often effective in psychotic depression. Worked example: Mr Banerjee, 68, stops eating and insists he has no stomach and is already dead. Option a is right because nihilistic delusions are characteristically seen in severe depression, where they express its themes of hopelessness, guilt and decay.

traps.b: Schizophrenia typically features persecutory delusions, delusions of reference, bizarre delusions, passivity and thought alienation experiences, and auditory hallucinations. When an exam asks which disorder delusions of nihilism, guilt or poverty point to, the answer is severe depression.
traps.c: Obsessive-compulsive disorder involves intrusive, unwanted obsessions (contamination, harm, symmetry) and compulsions performed to reduce anxiety. Obsessions are usually recognised as products of one's own mind and are resisted. DSM-5-TR has an insight specifier, 'with absent insight/delusional beliefs', yet even then the belief concerns the feared consequence, not the non-existence of self or world. It tempts because both involve distressing, persistent thoughts.
traps.d: Somatoform disorders (the DSM-IV and ICD-10 term; now somatic symptom and related disorders in DSM-5-TR and bodily distress disorder in ICD-11) involve distressing bodily symptoms with excessive health-related thoughts or worry. It tempts because nihilistic delusions often concern the body, such as 'my bowels are gone'.

q: Which theory of emotion contends that arousal and appraisal are independent processes brought about by the action of the thalamus?
concept: The answer is b: the Cannon-Bard theory holds that arousal and the experience of emotion are independent, simultaneous processes triggered by the thalamus. Walter Cannon (1927) and his student Philip Bard (1928) attacked the earlier James-Lange theory, which said that bodily arousal comes first and the felt emotion is our perception of it (we are afraid because we tremble). Cannon raised several objections: animals whose viscera were surgically cut off from the brain still showed emotional behaviour; the same visceral changes occur in fear, anger, fever and exercise, so they cannot tell emotions apart; the viscera respond too slowly to explain the speed of emotion; and injecting adrenaline produces arousal without a true emotion. In the Cannon-Bard view, an emotional stimulus is relayed through the thalamus, which sends signals at the same time upward to the cortex, producing the conscious feeling (the 'appraisal' of the stem), and downward to the body through the hypothalamus and autonomic nervous system, producing arousal. Neither causes the other. When Riya sees a snake on the path to her hostel, she feels fear and her heart races at the same instant, each from the thalamic signal. Bard's work on decorticate cats showed that 'sham rage' depended on the hypothalamus, which later shifted the centre downward, but the textbook theory still names the thalamus. Option b is right because only Cannon-Bard makes feeling and arousal independent and simultaneous via the thalamus. Exam trap: the Schachter-Singer theory also speaks of arousal and appraisal, but it makes them interact, with a cognitive label interpreting the arousal, rather than run independently.

traps.a: The James-Lange theory (William James, 1884; Carl Lange, 1885) makes bodily arousal come first and the emotion its perception, so the two are sequential and dependent, not independent. It gives the thalamus no special role.
traps.c: The Schachter-Singer two-factor theory (Stanley Schachter and Jerome Singer, 1962) says emotion is general arousal plus a cognitive label drawn from the situation, so the two factors interact. It is a cognitive theory, not a thalamic one.
traps.d: Activation theory (Donald Lindsley, 1951) places emotion on a continuum of arousal produced by the brainstem reticular activating system. It concerns the level of arousal, not independent thalamic signals.

q: The following is a part of the Peripheral Nervous System:
concept: The answer is c: the intercostal nerves are part of the peripheral nervous system. The nervous system has two main divisions. The central nervous system (CNS) is the brain and spinal cord, protected by bone, the meninges and cerebrospinal fluid. The peripheral nervous system (PNS) is everything outside them: the 12 pairs of cranial nerves, the 31 pairs of spinal nerves with their branches, and the ganglia. The PNS carries sensory information in and motor commands out, and is itself divided into the somatic nervous system (skin, skeletal muscle, voluntary movement) and the autonomic nervous system (internal organs, with sympathetic and parasympathetic branches). The intercostal nerves are the front branches (anterior rami) of the thoracic spinal nerves T1 to T11, running in the spaces between the ribs. They supply the intercostal muscles used in breathing and the skin of the chest and abdominal wall. Because they lie outside the spinal cord, they belong to the PNS, mainly to its somatic division. Example: Arjun develops shingles in one band across his chest. The virus has reactivated in the dorsal root ganglion of a thoracic spinal nerve and spread along its intercostal nerve, a peripheral structure. Option c is right because it is the only named structure that lies outside the brain and spinal cord. Exam trap: the three distractors come from different levels of the brain (midbrain from the brainstem, cerebellum from the hindbrain, thalamus from the diencephalon), so students who think 'not the cerebrum, therefore peripheral' fall into them. Every part of the brain, however deep or low, is CNS.

traps.a: The midbrain (mesencephalon) is part of the brainstem, containing the tectum and the substantia nigra; as a part of the brain it belongs to the central nervous system.
traps.b: The cerebellum, in the hindbrain, coordinates balance, posture and smooth movement; it is a brain structure and so part of the CNS.
traps.d: The thalamus, in the diencephalon, is the relay station for most sensory information on its way to the cortex; it is a brain structure and so part of the CNS.

q: Which therapy is most effective for Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD)?

options.b: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) with Exposure and Response Prevention

concept: The answer is b: cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) with exposure and response prevention (ERP) is the most effective psychological treatment for obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD). In OCD, intrusive obsessions (for example, 'my hands are contaminated') raise anxiety, and compulsions such as washing or checking bring brief relief. That relief negatively reinforces the compulsion, so the person never learns that the feared outcome would not happen and that anxiety falls on its own. ERP was introduced by the British psychologist Victor Meyer in 1966 and later refined by Edna Foa and others. It has two parts: exposure, in which the client faces the feared cue step by step up a hierarchy, and response prevention, in which the client deliberately does not perform the ritual. Anxiety then falls through habituation and extinction, and the obsession loses its power. Cognitive work is often added to tackle beliefs such as inflated responsibility or the overimportance of thoughts. Example: a woman who washes her hands 40 times a day touches a door handle and then refrains from washing for an hour, rating her anxiety as it peaks and then drops; over weeks the urge weakens. Option b is right because clinical guidelines (for example, NICE in the United Kingdom) recommend CBT including ERP as the first-line psychological treatment for OCD, often alongside SSRIs. Exam trap: insight-oriented therapies sound attractive because obsessions seem 'deep', but OCD responds to behavioural exposure, not interpretation.

traps.a: Psychoanalysis, Freud's insight therapy, explained obsessional neurosis through anal-stage conflicts (the Rat Man case, 1909), but it lacks controlled evidence for OCD and does not target the obsession and compulsion cycle.
traps.c: Client-centred therapy is Carl Rogers's non-directive approach built on empathy, genuineness and unconditional positive regard; it is supportive but not an evidence-based treatment for OCD symptoms.
traps.d: Gestalt therapy, from Fritz Perls, Laura Perls and Paul Goodman, builds here-and-now awareness with methods such as the empty chair; it has no established evidence for OCD.

q: Which symptom is considered a disorder of possession of thought?
concept: The answer is a: thought insertion is a disorder of the possession of thought. British descriptive psychopathology, especially Frank Fish's Clinical Psychopathology, which many Indian syllabuses follow, describes thought under four headings: stream (the speed and flow of thinking), form (how ideas are linked), content (what is thought, such as delusions) and possession (the sense that one's thoughts are one's own). Normally we take for granted that our thoughts belong to us and are under our control. In disorders of possession this ownership breaks down. Thought alienation has three classic forms: thought insertion (thoughts are put into the mind by an outside agency), thought withdrawal (thoughts are taken out) and thought broadcasting (thoughts pass out of the mind so that others know them). All three are first-rank symptoms of Kurt Schneider and strongly suggest schizophrenia in the absence of organic disease. Many Indian texts also place obsessions under possession, since the thought is known to be one's own yet cannot be controlled. Example: a patient says, 'These thoughts about killing are not mine; my neighbour beams them into my head with a machine.' The thoughts are experienced as foreign, not merely unwanted. Option a is right because thought insertion is a loss of ownership of thought, the defining feature of a possession disorder. Exam trap: circumstantiality, flight of ideas and tangentiality concern how thoughts flow and connect, so they are disorders of the stream or form of thought; and an obsession, unlike an inserted thought, is recognised as coming from one's own mind.

traps.b: Circumstantiality is speech loaded with needless detail and digressions that does finally reach its goal, seen in epilepsy, obsessional and organic states; it is a disorder of the form (or, in many Indian texts, the stream) of thought.
traps.c: Flight of ideas, typical of mania, is rapid thought that jumps from one idea to the next before any is finished, with links of chance, rhyme or clang that can still be traced; it is a disorder of the stream or form of thought.
traps.d: Tangentiality is answering obliquely and drifting away from the question without ever reaching the goal, seen in schizophrenia and mania; it is a disorder of the form or stream of thought, not of ownership.

q: Who developed the Filter-attenuation theory?
concept: The correct answer is Treisman. Anne Treisman proposed the attenuation theory (the filter-attenuation model) of selective attention in 1964 as a refinement of Donald Broadbent's earlier filter theory. Broadbent's filter model held that attention works like an all-or-nothing gate at an early stage: the unattended channel is blocked completely, so its content is not processed for meaning. However, this could not explain findings such as the cocktail party effect (named by Colin Cherry, 1953; the own-name finding is Neville Moray's, 1959), where a person attending to one conversation will still notice their own name spoken in an unattended conversation; if the unattended channel were fully blocked, the name could never get through. Treisman solved this by replacing the all-or-nothing filter with an attenuator. In her model the unattended message is not completely blocked but merely turned down or weakened (attenuated), so it still receives some processing. Words with low thresholds for activation, such as one's own name or highly salient or expected words, can still break through the attenuated channel and reach awareness. This elegantly accounts for why we mostly ignore unattended input yet occasionally catch personally significant items. Treisman's attenuation theory is therefore the filter-attenuation model the question refers to.

traps.a: Broadbent developed the original filter (early-selection) theory, in which the unattended channel is completely blocked, not merely attenuated.
traps.c: Johnston (with Heinz) proposed a flexible/multimode model of attention, not the filter-attenuation theory.
traps.d: Heinz is associated with the multimode theory of attention, not the attenuation model, which is Treisman's.

q: Which of the following is not based on operant conditioning?
concept: The answer is b: implosion is not based on operant conditioning; it rests on classical conditioning and extinction. Operant conditioning, set out by B. F. Skinner (1938), changes behaviour through its consequences: reinforcement makes a response more likely, punishment less likely. Implosive therapy (Thomas Stampfl and Donald Levis, 1967) instead targets a conditioned fear. The client imagines the most feared scenes at full, exaggerated intensity, often enriched with horrific or psychodynamic themes, for a long session with no escape. Its logic comes from O. Hobart Mowrer's (1947) two-factor theory: fear is learned by classical conditioning, and avoidance keeps it alive. When the feared cue (the conditioned stimulus) is met again and again without the dreaded outcome (the unconditioned stimulus), the fear extinguishes. Flooding applies the same idea, usually in real life; implosion is flooding in imagination, and it is rarely used now. Example: Arjun, terrified of snakes, is asked to picture for an hour snakes coiling round him and biting, while the therapist keeps the scenes vivid and blocks every escape; his fear peaks and then falls. The other three are operant. Contingency management gives reinforcers, such as vouchers, for a verified target behaviour, such as drug-free urine samples. A token economy (Teodoro Ayllon and Nathan Azrin, 1968) gives tokens for target behaviours that are exchanged for back-up rewards. The Premack principle (David Premack, 1959) says a more probable activity can reinforce a less probable one. Option b is right because implosion works by extinguishing a classically conditioned fear, not by arranging consequences. Exam trap: all four are behaviour therapy techniques, so 'behavioural' does not decide the answer; ask whether the method arranges consequences (operant) or pairs and unpairs stimuli (classical).

traps.c: A token economy (Teodoro Ayllon and Nathan Azrin, 1968) is operant: tokens, which are secondary reinforcers, are earned for target behaviours and exchanged for back-up reinforcers, as first done on psychiatric wards.
traps.d: The Premack principle (David Premack, 1959) is an operant rule: a more probable activity reinforces a less probable one, as in 'finish your homework, then play cricket'.

Implosive therapy (Thomas Stampfl and Donald Levis, 1967) instead targets a conditioned fear. The client imagines the most feared scenes at full, exaggerated intensity, often enriched with horrific or psychodynamic themes, for a long session with no escape. Its logic comes from O. Hobart Mowrer's (1947) two-factor theory: fear is learned by classical conditioning, and avoidance keeps it alive. When the feared cue (the conditioned stimulus) is met again and again without the dreaded outcome (the unconditioned stimulus), the fear extinguishes. Flooding applies the same idea, usually in real life; implosion is flooding in imagination, and it is rarely used now. Example: Arjun, terrified of snakes, is asked to picture for an hour snakes coiling round him and biting, while the therapist keeps the scenes vivid and blocks every escape; his fear peaks and then falls. The other three are operant. Contingency management gives reinforcers, such as vouchers, for a verified target behaviour, such as drug-free urine samples. A token economy (Teodoro Ayllon and Nathan Azrin, 1968) gives tokens for target behaviours that are exchanged for back-up rewards. The Premack principle (David Premack, 1959) says a more probable activity can reinforce a less probable one. Option b is right because implosion works by extinguishing a classically conditioned fear, not by arranging consequences. Exam trap: all four are behaviour therapy techniques, so 'behavioural' does not decide the answer; ask whether the method arranges consequences (operant) or pairs and unpairs stimuli (classical).

q: Which of the following best describes delusion?

options.b: A fixed false belief not amenable to reason

concept: The answer is b: a delusion is a fixed false belief not amenable to reason. In descriptive psychopathology a delusion is a false, firmly held belief that is not shaken by argument or contrary evidence and is out of keeping with the person's cultural, religious and educational background. Karl Jaspers, in General Psychopathology (1913), named its three external marks: subjective certainty, incorrigibility (it cannot be corrected by experience or reasoning) and impossibility or falsity of content. The cultural clause matters: a community's shared belief in the evil eye or in spirits is not a delusion, however strange it seems to an outsider. Delusions are disorders of thought content, not of perception. They can be primary (not understandable from any other experience) or secondary (understandable from a mood or hallucination), and they are classified by theme: persecutory (the commonest), reference, grandiose, nihilistic, guilt, jealousy, erotomania and somatic. Together with hallucinations and disorganised speech or behaviour, delusions mark psychosis. Example: a clerk is utterly convinced that his neighbours have planted cameras in his walls to steal his ideas; when shown that no cameras exist, he says they have been cleverly hidden. Option b is right because fixity and imperviousness to reason are the defining features of a delusion. Exam trap: an overvalued idea (Carl Wernicke's term) is also a strongly held belief, but it is understandable and lacks absolute fixity, as in the anorexic patient's conviction that she is fat; an obsession is recognised as one's own and resisted.

traps.a: A perceptual disturbance is a hallucination or illusion, a disorder of perception; a delusion is a disorder of the content of thought, a belief, not a perception.
traps.c: A mood disorder is a diagnostic category (depression, bipolar disorder), not a symptom; delusions can occur within severe mood disorders but are not defined by mood.
traps.d: An obsession is an intrusive, unwanted thought that the person recognises as their own and as senseless, and tries to resist, as in OCD; a delusion is held with full conviction and not resisted.

q: The primary focus of Behavior Therapy is:
concept: The answer is d: the primary focus of behaviour therapy is changing problem behaviour patterns through the principles of conditioning. Behaviour therapy applies laws of learning first worked out in the laboratory. Classical conditioning comes from Ivan Pavlov (1927): a neutral stimulus paired with one that already produces a response comes to produce it alone. Operant conditioning comes from B. F. Skinner (1938): behaviour followed by reinforcement becomes more frequent, and behaviour that is not reinforced fades. John B. Watson and Rosalie Rayner (1920) conditioned fear in Little Albert, and Mary Cover Jones (1924) removed a boy's fear of rabbits by pairing the rabbit with food. Hans Eysenck (1952) then argued that insight therapy had not been shown to work, and Joseph Wolpe (1958) offered systematic desensitisation, pairing relaxation with a graded fear hierarchy. The approach assumes that problem behaviour is learned by the same rules as normal behaviour and can be unlearned. The behaviour itself is the problem, not a sign of hidden conflict, and what keeps it going now matters more than how it began. Treatment starts with a functional analysis of antecedents, behaviour and consequences (the ABC model), and progress is measured against a baseline. Example: Meera fears dogs. Her therapist teaches her to relax, then moves her step by step from pictures of dogs to a puppy on a lead, praising each step; her fear fades through counterconditioning and extinction. Option d is right because conditioning, classical and operant, is the defining tool of behaviour therapy. Exam trap: changing thoughts is cognitive therapy (Aaron Beck, 1976; Albert Ellis, 1962), and adding the word 'unconscious' turns it into psychoanalysis; neither is behaviour therapy, which works on observable behaviour.

traps.a: Making unconscious material conscious is the aim of Sigmund Freud's psychoanalysis (The Interpretation of Dreams, 1900); behaviour therapy deliberately sets aside hypothesised unconscious causes.
traps.b: Personal growth and self-actualisation are the focus of humanistic therapy, Carl Rogers's person-centred therapy (1951) and Abraham Maslow's theory (1954), not of conditioning-based treatment.
traps.c: Exploring early childhood experience is the psychodynamic route to insight; behaviour therapy concentrates on what maintains a behaviour now, not on its distant origins.

q: The apparent lack of empathy and the tendency to exploit others for self-benefit have led psychologists to compare narcissistic personality disorder with which one of the following?
concept: The answer is b: narcissistic personality disorder is often compared with antisocial personality disorder (APD), because both show a lack of empathy and a readiness to exploit others for personal gain. Both are Cluster B (dramatic, emotional, erratic) disorders in DSM-5. Narcissistic personality disorder is a pervasive pattern of grandiosity, need for admiration and lack of empathy; two of its nine criteria are being interpersonally exploitative (taking advantage of others to achieve one's own ends) and lacking empathy. APD is a pervasive pattern of disregard for and violation of the rights of others since age 15, with deceitfulness, impulsivity, aggression, irresponsibility and lack of remorse. The overlap is strong enough that Otto Kernberg (1984) described malignant narcissism, a severe form in which narcissism mixes with antisocial behaviour, aggression and paranoid traits, and Robert Hare's psychopathy checklist (PCL-R, 1991) includes a grandiose sense of self-worth. The difference lies in motive and style: the narcissist exploits mainly to protect an inflated but fragile self-image and win admiration, while the antisocial person exploits for material gain or thrills, often breaking the law. Example: Vikram takes credit for a junior's report because he believes he deserves the spotlight (narcissistic); his cousin forges his employer's signature to take money, then shrugs it off (antisocial). Option b is right because lack of empathy and exploitation are core features shared by narcissistic and antisocial personality disorders. Exam trap: histrionic personality disorder (a) is also Cluster B and also craves attention, but its hallmark is emotional, seductive display, not cold exploitation, so it is only the near miss.

traps.a: Histrionic personality disorder (Cluster B) is excessive emotionality and attention-seeking, often seductive and theatrical; it shares a need for attention with narcissism but not the cold exploitation seen in APD.
traps.c: Paranoid personality disorder (Cluster A) is pervasive distrust and suspicion, reading others' motives as malevolent; its core is suspicion, not exploitation.
traps.d: Schizotypal personality disorder (Cluster A) involves odd beliefs, magical thinking, eccentric behaviour and social anxiety; it belongs to the schizophrenia spectrum, not to exploitation.

q: When a counsellor repeats what the client says, but uses words that are different than what the client used, the counsellor is using what skill?
concept: The correct answer is paraphrasing. Paraphrasing (also called reflection of content or restatement) is a core microskill in counselling, systematised within the microcounselling framework of Allen Ivey and prominent in the person-centred tradition of Carl Rogers. It involves the counsellor listening carefully and then restating the essential content or meaning of what the client has just said, but in the counsellor's own, different words rather than simply parroting the client's exact phrasing. Effective paraphrasing serves several purposes: it demonstrates to the client that the counsellor is listening and understands, it checks the accuracy of the counsellor's understanding (allowing the client to correct any misinterpretation), it helps the client hear their own thoughts reflected back and thereby clarify them, and it conveys empathy and builds rapport. It is distinct from reflection of feeling, which mirrors the client's emotions rather than content, and from summarising, which condenses a longer stretch of material. The distractors name other skills: questioning gathers information, empathy is the broader attitude of understanding (which paraphrasing helps express), and nonverbal communication concerns body language and tone. Because the described skill specifically involves restating the client's words differently, paraphrasing is correct. This item tests knowledge of basic counselling microskills.

traps.b: Questioning involves posing questions to gather information or prompt reflection, not restating the client's message in different words.
traps.c: Empathy is the deeper capacity to understand and share the client's feelings; paraphrasing is one specific verbal technique that can convey empathy, but the skill described here is specifically paraphrasing.
traps.d: Nonverbal communication refers to body language, tone, and gestures, not to the verbal restatement of the client's words.

q: Which of the following are not included in the ICD criteria for Schizophrenia?
concept: The correct answer is catastrophic thinking, because it is NOT a diagnostic criterion for schizophrenia. Schizophrenia is defined in classification systems such as the ICD (International Classification of Diseases) and the DSM by a characteristic set of positive symptoms (excesses or distortions of normal function) and negative symptoms (reductions in normal function). The core positive symptoms that feature in the diagnostic criteria include delusions (fixed false beliefs, such as persecutory or grandiose delusions), hallucinations (perceptions without external stimuli, most commonly auditory hallucinations such as hearing voices), and disorganised speech or thinking (formal thought disorder, evident as derailment, tangentiality, or incoherence). Grossly disorganised or catatonic behaviour and negative symptoms such as flattened affect and avolition also count. Kurt Schneider's first-rank symptoms historically informed these criteria. Catastrophic thinking, by contrast, is a cognitive distortion in which a person assumes the worst possible outcome will occur. It is characteristic of anxiety disorders and depression and is a target of cognitive therapy in the tradition of Aaron Beck, but it is not part of the schizophrenia criteria. The item tests the student's ability to separate the defining psychotic symptoms of schizophrenia from a cognitive distortion belonging to the anxiety and mood disorders.

traps.a: Delusions are a core positive symptom and a central diagnostic criterion for schizophrenia in both ICD and DSM.
traps.c: Disorganised speech (formal thought disorder) is a recognised diagnostic feature of schizophrenia.
traps.d: Hallucinations, especially auditory ones, are a hallmark positive symptom and key criterion for schizophrenia.

q: A patient presents with fluctuating levels of consciousness, visual hallucinations, and autonomic dysfunction. Which condition is most likely?
concept: The answer is b: fluctuating consciousness, visual hallucinations and autonomic dysfunction point to dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB). Lewy bodies are abnormal clumps of the protein alpha-synuclein inside neurons, named after Friedrich Lewy, who described them in 1912 in Parkinson's disease. In DLB they spread through the cortex as well as the brainstem. The consensus criteria of Ian McKeith and colleagues (fourth report, 2017) list four core clinical features: fluctuating cognition with marked variation in attention and alertness; recurrent, well-formed visual hallucinations; REM sleep behaviour disorder, in which the person acts out dreams; and parkinsonism (slowness, rigidity, tremor). Supportive features include severe sensitivity to antipsychotics, repeated falls, fainting and autonomic dysfunction such as low blood pressure on standing, constipation and urinary incontinence. Memory may be fairly spared early, while attention, executive and visuospatial skills fail first. Example: a 72-year-old man is lucid one afternoon and drowsy and confused the next, sees small children sitting in his living room, has shouted and kicked in his sleep for years, feels faint on standing and walks with a shuffle. Option b is right because fluctuation, vivid visual hallucinations and autonomic problems together fit DLB and none of the other options. Exam trap: severe antipsychotic sensitivity is the safety point examiners love, since a typical antipsychotic given for the hallucinations can cause dangerous, even fatal, worsening of rigidity and confusion. Delirium also fluctuates, but it is acute and is not offered here.

traps.a: Schizophrenia usually begins in late adolescence or early adulthood with mainly auditory hallucinations and delusions in clear consciousness; fluctuating alertness and autonomic failure are not features.
traps.c: Major depressive disorder involves low mood or loss of interest for at least two weeks; psychotic depression can add mood-congruent hallucinations, but not a fluctuating level of consciousness with autonomic dysfunction.
traps.d: OCD consists of obsessions and compulsions with intact consciousness and insight usually preserved; it has no hallucinations, fluctuation or autonomic syndrome.
